original:
- Mitochondrial & Cellular Energy Starvation (Glutamine, Butyrate, TCA Intermediates): Your gut barrier requires massive amounts of immediate, localized energy to maintain tight junction integrity. If your enterocytes (small intestine) or colonocytes (large intestine) lack their preferred mitochondrial fuels, the barrier structurally collapses, allowing lipopolysaccharides (LPS) and endotoxins to leak into systemic circulation.

    - L-Glutamine ([watch Dr. Rhonda vid](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=5DVUEKrekYw&ra=m)): The absolute premier energy substrate for enterocytes and activated immune cells. It bypasses complex digestive steps, converting directly into alpha-ketoglutarate (α-KG) inside the mitochondria to power the citric acid cycle. This immediate cellular energy hit actively drives the repair of the gut mucosal barrier and prevents LPS translocation.

      - Dosing: Use 5g daily as a baseline to counter the gut mucosal breakdown caused by high-intensity or high-volume training (like CrossFit or intense cardio). Titrate up to 10–30g daily during acute immune exposure, high systemic stress, or if you are dealing with active IBD (Crohn's/Colitis).

      - The Cancer Caveat: Because hyper-proliferative cancer cells can also hijack glutamine to fuel their rapid replication, avoid high-dose protocol titrations if you have an active, existing colon or liver malignancy (the liver sees it first via portal vein delivery).

    - Butyrate & SCFAs: While the small intestine runs on glutamine, the large intestine relies on short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like butyrate. Getting these via raw resistant starch fermentation or your home-brewed SIBO yogurt fuels colonocytes, locks down the lower gut barrier, and systematically suppresses inflammatory signals.

    - TCA Cycle Intermediates (Malic & Citric Acid): Organic acids like malate and citrate feed directly into the exact same mitochondrial energy pathways as glutamine. Consuming clean, sour profiles—such as organic malic acid, tart cherries, or green apples—provides rapid, alternative fuel to gut epithelial cells, accelerating mucosal healing from a different biochemical angle.
rewrite:
- Mitochondrial and cellular energy starvation is what you get when there's not enough of the fuels each type of cell in your gut prefers (glutamine, butyrate, TCA intermediates). Your gut barrier needs a lot of energy, to keep its tight junctions intact. If the cells lining your small intestine (called enterocytes) or the colonocytes lining your large intestine don't do that, the barrier loosens up. Then lipopolysaccharides (LPS, which come from the walls of bacteria) and other endotoxins leak through those (not-so-tight)-junction gaps into your bloodstream.

- L-Glutamine ([watch Dr. Rhonda vid](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=5DVUEKrekYw&ra=m)) is the main fuel your enterocytes run on, and your immune cells use it too when they're activated. It skips the complicated digestive steps other nutrients have to go through. Inside the mitochondria it gets turned straight into alpha-ketoglutarate (α-KG), which feeds the citric acid cycle, where the mitochondria make their energy. So the cells get that energy right away, and that's what drives the repair of the gut lining and keeps LPS from slipping through.

- Take 5g a day as a baseline. The point of that baseline is to counter the breakdown of the gut lining that high-intensity or high-volume training causes, like CrossFit or intense cardio. If your immune system is dealing with an acute exposure, if your whole system is under a lot of stress, or if you have active IBD (Crohn's or colitis), raise it gradually to 10-30g a day.

- CAUTION: cancer cells that multiply really fast can grab glutamine too, to fuel their growth. So if you have an active colon or liver cancer, don't raise the dose that high. The liver is on that list because it's where the glutamine goes first, through the portal vein.

- Butyrate and the other short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are what your colon runs on, the way your small intestine runs on glutamine. You get them when your gut bacteria ferment raw resistant starch, or from your home-brewed SIBO yogurt. They feed the colonocytes and tighten up the lower gut barrier, and they keep turning down inflammatory signals too.

- TCA cycle intermediates, like malic and citric acid, are organic acids that go into the same energy pathways in the mitochondria that glutamine does. So clean sour stuff like organic malic acid, tart cherries or green apples gives the cells lining your gut another quick fuel, and it speeds up healing of the lining, just by a different biochemical route than glutamine.
